Charles I. King of England, Scotland, and Ireland from 1625 until his execution in 1649. His belief in the divine right of kings and his constant power struggles with Parliament led directly to the English Civil War, one of the most consequential conflicts in British history. Following the defeat of the Royalist forces, he was tried, convicted of high treason, and executed, resulting in the brief abolition of the monarchy itself.

Charles was executed by beheading in 1649 outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, London. His downfall had roots in his governance long before the civil war. He ruled without Parliament for eleven years between 1629 and 1640, a period known as the Personal Rule or the Eleven Years' Tyranny. During this time, he levied the controversial Ship Money tax during peacetime, attempting to fund the navy without parliamentary consent, which outraged the public. He further inflamed tensions by triggering the Bishops' Wars when he attempted to force the Anglican Book of Common Prayer on the Presbyterian Church of Scotland.

When civil war finally came, Charles was defeated by the Parliamentarian New Model Army led by generals like Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell. His father had been James I, who attempted to claim the title King of Great Britain. Cromwell would later serve as Lord Protector during the Commonwealth era that followed Charles's death, and the interregnum left an indelible mark on the British understanding of monarchy and constitutional governance.
